# arbitrary 1.4.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/latest/source/README.md

```

The `Arbitrary` crate lets you construct arbitrary instances of a type.
This crate is primarily intended to be combined with a fuzzer like [libFuzzer
and `cargo-fuzz`](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) or
[AFL](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/afl.rs), and to help you turn the raw,
untyped byte buffers that they produce into well-typed, valid, structured
values. This allows you to combine structure-aware test case generation with
coverage-guided, mutation-based fuzzers.
[**Read the API documentation on `docs.rs`!**](https://docs.rs/arbitrary)
Say you're writing a color conversion library, and you have an `Rgb` struct to
represent RGB colors. You might want to implement `Arbitrary` for `Rgb` so that
you could take arbitrary `Rgb` instances in a test function that asserts some
property (for example, asserting that RGB converted to HSL and converted back to
RGB always ends up exactly where we started).
Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to implement
`Arbitrary` for your types.
Automatically deriving `Arbitrary` requires you to enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature:
```toml
[dependencies]
arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```
And then you can simply add `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotations to your types:
```rust
// rgb.rs
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
pub struct Rgb {
}
```
This can be particular handy if your structure uses a type that does not implement `Arbitrary` or you want to have more customization for particular fields.
```rust
pub struct Rgba {
}
fn arbitrary_b(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<u8> {
}
```
Alternatively, you can write an `Arbitrary` implementation by hand:
```rust
// rgb.rs
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
pub struct Rgb {
}
impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for Rgb {
}
```
This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust **1.63.0** and up. It might
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.
We reserve the right to increment the MSRV on minor releases, however we will
strive to only do it deliberately and for good reasons.
Licensed under dual MIT or Apache-2.0 at your choice.
Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in this project by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license,
shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.
```

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`

- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`

- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`

- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)- `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse2](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html)- file - `full`and- `parsing`
- Parse the content of a file of Rust code.

# exhaustigen 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/exhaustigen/0.1.0

## Exhaustigen

This is a tiny (but delightful!) utility library for exhaustive testing.

It is based (directly) on the idea and code in the following blog post:

TL;DR: the idea is to write a test that is *similar* to the sort of test one
writes against a PRNG -- an imperative test that just asks some "generator" to
create scalars, booleans, data vectors, random shuffles, etc. -- but to use a
special generator that has some interesting features:

- It has a concept of being "done", so you can put it in a do-while loop
- Every call to it requires an inclusive upper bound, which should be small
- It *tracks its progress*through the sequence of bounds
- It *lazily extends*the sequence of bounds as it's asked for more data

By threading such a generator through such an imperative test, and putting the body of that test in a do-while loop, you can write straightforward code with elaborate value-dependent nesting structure -- eg. generate value K in 0..N and then value J in 0..K and so forth -- and it will automatically record and enumerate the space of sequences meaningful to the code, re-running until it has exhausted all possible paths/values.

## License

MIT + ASL2.0, with permission from Aleksey.

Returns `true` when every range of values implied by calls to `gen` is
finished. Otherwise restarts the innermost incomplete range, continuing
the exhaustive scan. This method should be called in the head of a
`while` loop enclosing the test you wish to repeat exhaustively.

Returns a value (eventually every value) between 0 and `bound`
inclusive. Every other value-generating method in this type ultimately
funnels into this method, which is responsible (in concert with `done`)
for opening ang stepping through ranges of the generator’s state-space.

Selects an element (eventually every element) from `input`.

# arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/latest/target-redirect/arbitrary/index.html

## Expand description

The `Arbitrary` trait crate.

This trait provides an [ Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html) trait to
produce well-typed, structured values, from raw, byte buffers. It is
generally intended to be used with fuzzers like AFL or libFuzzer. See the

[trait’s documentation for details on automatically deriving, implementing, and/or using the trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`Arbitrary`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [size_](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html)- hint
- Utilities for working with and combining the results of
`Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [unstructured](https://docs.rs/unstructured/index.html)
- Wrappers around raw, unstructured bytes.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [MaxRecursion](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)- Reached
- Error indicating that the maximum recursion depth has been reached while calculating `Arbitrary::size_hint`
- [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)
- A source of unstructured data.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An enumeration of buffer creation errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A `Result`with the error type fixed as`arbitrary::Error`.

[63](https://docs.rs#63)/// implement `Arbitrary` for your types.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)///
[65](https://docs.rs#65)/// Using the custom derive requires that you enable the `"derive"` cargo
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// feature in your `Cargo.toml`:
[67](https://docs.rs#67)///
[68](https://docs.rs#68)/// ```toml
[69](https://docs.rs#69)/// [dependencies]
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)/// ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)///
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// Then, you add the `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotation to your `struct` or
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// `enum` type definition:
[75](https://docs.rs#75)///
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// ```
[77](https://docs.rs#77)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
[79](https://docs.rs#79)/// use std::collections::HashSet;
[80](https://docs.rs#80)///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// pub struct AddressBook {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///     friends: HashSet<Friend>,
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// }
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// #[derive(Arbitrary, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// pub enum Friend {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///     Buddy { name: String },
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///     Pal { age: usize },
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// # }
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// ```
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// Every member of the `struct` or `enum` must also implement `Arbitrary`.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)///
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// It is also possible to change the default bounds added by the derive:
[97](https://docs.rs#97)///
[98](https://docs.rs#98)/// ```
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)/// use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
[101](https://docs.rs#101)///
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// trait Trait {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)///     type Assoc: for<'a> Arbitrary<'a>;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// }
[105](https://docs.rs#105)///
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// // The bounds are used verbatim, so any existing trait bounds will need to be repeated.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// #[arbitrary(bound = "T: Trait")]
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// struct Point<T: Trait> {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)///     x: T::Assoc,
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// # }
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// ```
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// # Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// Implementing `Arbitrary` mostly involves nested calls to other `Arbitrary`
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// arbitrary implementations for each of your `struct` or `enum`'s members. But
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// sometimes you need some amount of raw data, or you need to generate a
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// variably-sized collection type, or something of that sort. The
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// [`Unstructured`] type helps you with these tasks.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// ```
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] mod foo {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// # pub struct MyCollection<T> { _t: std::marker::PhantomData<T> }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// # impl<T> MyCollection<T> {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// #     pub fn new() -> Self { MyCollection { _t: std::marker::PhantomData } }
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// #     pub fn insert(&mut self, element: T) {}
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// # }
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// where
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///     T: Arbitrary<'a>,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///         // Get an iterator of arbitrary `T`s.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)///         let iter = u.arbitrary_iter::<T>()?;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///         // And then create a collection!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///         let mut my_collection = MyCollection::new();
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///         for elem_result in iter {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///             let elem = elem_result?;
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///             my_collection.insert(elem);
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///         }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///         Ok(my_collection)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///     }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// }
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// # }
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// ```
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// # A Note On Output Distributions
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// There is no requirement for a particular distribution of the values. For
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// example, it is not required that every value appears with the same
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// probability. That being said, the main use for `Arbitrary` is for fuzzing,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// so in many cases a uniform distribution will make the most sense in order to
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// provide the best coverage of the domain. In other cases this is not
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// desirable or even possible, for example when sampling from a uniform
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// distribution is computationally expensive or in the case of collections that
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// may grow indefinitely.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)pub trait Arbitrary<'a>: Sized {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the given unstructured data.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    ///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// Calling `Arbitrary::arbitrary` requires that you have some raw data,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// perhaps given to you by a fuzzer like AFL or libFuzzer. You wrap this
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// raw data in an `Unstructured`, and then you can call `<MyType as
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// Arbitrary>::arbitrary` to construct an arbitrary instance of `MyType`
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// from that unstructured data.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    ///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// Implementations may return an error if there is not enough data to
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// construct a full instance of `Self`, or they may fill out the rest of
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// `Self` with dummy values. Using dummy values when the underlying data is
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// exhausted can help avoid accidentally "defeating" some of the fuzzer's
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// mutations to the underlying byte stream that might otherwise lead to
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// interesting runtime behavior or new code coverage if only we had just a
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// few more bytes. However, it also requires that implementations for
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// recursive types (e.g. `struct Foo(Option<Box<Foo>>)`) avoid infinite
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// recursion when the underlying data is exhausted.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    ///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// # #[cfg(feature = "derive")] fn foo() {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    ///
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// #[derive(Arbitrary)]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// pub struct MyType {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    ///     // ...
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// // Get the raw data from the fuzzer or wherever else.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// # let get_raw_data_from_fuzzer = || &[];
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// let raw_data: &[u8] = get_raw_data_from_fuzzer();
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// // Wrap that raw data in an `Unstructured`.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// // Generate an arbitrary instance of `MyType` and do stuff with it.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// if let Ok(value) = MyType::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// #   let do_stuff = |_| {};
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    ///     do_stuff(value);
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// }
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// # }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// ```
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// See also the documentation for [`Unstructured`].
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self>;
[208](https://docs.rs#208)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the entirety of the given
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// unstructured data.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    ///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// This is similar to Arbitrary::arbitrary, however it assumes that it is
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// the last consumer of the given data, and is thus able to consume it all
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// if it needs.  See also the documentation for
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// [`Unstructured`].
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn arbitrary_take_rest(mut u: Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        Self::arbitrary(&mut u)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// needs to construct itself.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    ///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// This is useful for determining how many elements we should insert when
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// creating an arbitrary collection.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// The return value is similar to [`Iterator::size_hint`]: it returns a
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number of bytes
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// The default implementation return `(0, None)` which is correct for any
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    /// type, but not ultimately that useful. Using `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` will
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// create a better implementation. If you are writing an `Arbitrary`
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// implementation by hand, and your type can be part of a dynamically sized
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// collection (such as `Vec`), you are strongly encouraged to override this
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// default with a better implementation, and also override
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// [`try_size_hint`].
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ///
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    /// ## How to implement this
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    ///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// If the size hint calculation is a trivial constant and does not recurse
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// into any other `size_hint` call, you should implement it in `size_hint`:
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// ```
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    ///
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// struct SomeStruct(u8);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    ///         let buf = &mut [0];
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    ///         u.fill_buffer(buf)?;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ///         Ok(SomeStruct(buf[0]))
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///     }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    ///
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ///     #[inline]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    ///         let _ = depth;
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///         (1, Some(1))
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///     }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// Otherwise, it should instead be implemented in [`try_size_hint`],
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// and the `size_hint` implementation should forward to it:
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    ///
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Result, Unstructured};
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// struct SomeStruct<A, B> {
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///     a: A,
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    ///     b: B,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// impl<'a, A: Arbitrary<'a>, B: Arbitrary<'a>> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct<A, B> {
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///         // ...
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// #       todo!()
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///     }
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    ///
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    ///         // Return the value of try_size_hint
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    ///         //
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    ///         // If the recursion fails, return the default, always valid `(0, None)`
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    ///         Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///     }
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    ///
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    ///     fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ///         // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    ///         // `try_recursion_guard`.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    ///         size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///             // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    ///             // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///             // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ///             // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    ///             // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    ///             // accidentally use the wrong depth.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ///             Ok(size_hint::and(
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    ///                 <A as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///                 <B as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    ///             ))
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    ///         })
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    ///     }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// ```
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    ///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// ## Invariant
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    ///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// [`Arbitrary::arbitrary`] and [`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`].
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// space.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ///
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// [iterator-size-hint]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// [`try_size_hint`]: Arbitrary::try_size_hint
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    #[inline]
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        let _ = depth;
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        (0, None)
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// needs to construct itself.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    ///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// Unlike [`size_hint`], this function keeps the information that the
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// recursion limit was reached. This is required to "short circuit" the
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    /// calculation and avoid exponential blowup with recursive structures.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    ///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// If you are implementing [`size_hint`] for a struct that could be
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// recursive, you should implement `try_size_hint` and call the
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// `try_size_hint` when recursing
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// The return value is similar to [`core::iter::Iterator::size_hint`]: it
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// returns a tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// of bytes required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    ///
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// The default implementation returns the value of [`size_hint`] which is
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// correct for any type, but might lead to exponential blowup when dealing
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// with recursive types.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    ///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// ## Invariant
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    /// of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// [`Arbitrary::arbitrary`] and [`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`].
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// space.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    ///
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// ## When to implement `try_size_hint`
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    ///
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// If you 100% know that the type you are implementing `Arbitrary` for is
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// not a recursive type, or your implementation is not transitively calling
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// any other `size_hint` methods, you may implement [`size_hint`], and the
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// default `try_size_hint` implementation will use it.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    ///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Note that if you are implementing `Arbitrary` for a generic type, you
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// cannot guarantee the lack of type recursion!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// Otherwise, when there is possible type recursion, you should implement
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// `try_size_hint` instead.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// ## The `depth` parameter
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// When implementing `try_size_hint`, you need to use
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// [`arbitrary::size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth)`][crate::size_hint::try_recursion_guard]
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// to prevent potential infinite recursion when calculating size hints for
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// potentially recursive types:
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    ///
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// ```
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Unstructured};
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// // This can potentially be a recursive type if `L` or `R` contain
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// // something like `Box<Option<MyEither<L, R>>>`!
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// enum MyEither<L, R> {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    ///     Left(L),
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    ///     Right(R),
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// }
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    /// impl<'a, L, R> Arbitrary<'a> for MyEither<L, R>
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// where
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    ///     L: Arbitrary<'a>,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    ///     R: Arbitrary<'a>,
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///     fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<Self> {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    ///         // ...
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// #       unimplemented!()
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///     fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///         // Return the value of `try_size_hint`
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///         //
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    ///         // If the recursion fails, return the default `(0, None)` range,
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///         // which is always valid.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    ///         Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    ///     }
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    ///
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///     fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///         // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    ///         // `try_recursion_guard`.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    ///         size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    ///             // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///             // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    ///             // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///             // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    ///             // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///             // accidentally use the wrong depth.
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///             Ok(size_hint::or(
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///                 <L as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///                 <R as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///             ))
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///         })
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///     }
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// }
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// ```
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    #[inline]
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        Ok(Self::size_hint(depth))
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    }

}## Expand description

Generate arbitrary structured values from raw, unstructured data.

The `Arbitrary` trait allows you to generate valid structured values, like
`HashMap`s, or ASTs, or `MyTomlConfig`, or any other data structure from
raw, unstructured bytes provided by a fuzzer.

[§](https://docs.rs#deriving-arbitrary)Deriving `Arbitrary`

Automatically deriving the `Arbitrary` trait is the recommended way to
implement `Arbitrary` for your types.

Using the custom derive requires that you enable the `"derive"` cargo
feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```
Then, you add the `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` annotation to your `struct` or
`enum` type definition:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
use std::collections::HashSet;
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct AddressBook {
    friends: HashSet<Friend>,
}
#[derive(Arbitrary, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum Friend {
    Buddy { name: String },
    Pal { age: usize },
}
```
Every member of the `struct` or `enum` must also implement `Arbitrary`.

It is also possible to change the default bounds added by the derive:

```
use arbitrary::Arbitrary;
trait Trait {
    type Assoc: for<'a> Arbitrary<'a>;
}
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
// The bounds are used verbatim, so any existing trait bounds will need to be repeated.
#[arbitrary(bound = "T: Trait")]
struct Point<T: Trait> {
    x: T::Assoc,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-arbitrary-by-hand)Implementing `Arbitrary` By Hand

Implementing `Arbitrary` mostly involves nested calls to other `Arbitrary`
arbitrary implementations for each of your `struct` or `enum`’s members. But
sometimes you need some amount of raw data, or you need to generate a
variably-sized collection type, or something of that sort. The
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html) type helps you with these tasks.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
where
    T: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // Get an iterator of arbitrary `T`s.
        let iter = u.arbitrary_iter::<T>()?;
        // And then create a collection!
        let mut my_collection = MyCollection::new();
        for elem_result in iter {
            let elem = elem_result?;
            my_collection.insert(elem);
        }
        Ok(my_collection)
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#a-note-on-output-distributions)A Note On Output Distributions

There is no requirement for a particular distribution of the values. For
example, it is not required that every value appears with the same
probability. That being said, the main use for `Arbitrary` is for fuzzing,
so in many cases a uniform distribution will make the most sense in order to
provide the best coverage of the domain. In other cases this is not
desirable or even possible, for example when sampling from a uniform
distribution is computationally expensive or in the case of collections that
may grow indefinitely.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#207)

#### fn [arbitrary](https://docs.rs#tymethod.arbitrary)(u: &mut [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the given unstructured data.

Calling `Arbitrary::arbitrary` requires that you have some raw data,
perhaps given to you by a fuzzer like AFL or libFuzzer. You wrap this
raw data in an `Unstructured`, and then you can call `<MyType as Arbitrary>::arbitrary` to construct an arbitrary instance of `MyType`
from that unstructured data.

Implementations may return an error if there is not enough data to
construct a full instance of `Self`, or they may fill out the rest of
`Self` with dummy values. Using dummy values when the underlying data is
exhausted can help avoid accidentally “defeating” some of the fuzzer’s
mutations to the underlying byte stream that might otherwise lead to
interesting runtime behavior or new code coverage if only we had just a
few more bytes. However, it also requires that implementations for
recursive types (e.g. `struct Foo(Option<Box<Foo>>)`) avoid infinite
recursion when the underlying data is exhausted.

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct MyType {
    // ...
}
// Get the raw data from the fuzzer or wherever else.
let raw_data: &[u8] = get_raw_data_from_fuzzer();
// Wrap that raw data in an `Unstructured`.
let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
// Generate an arbitrary instance of `MyType` and do stuff with it.
if let Ok(value) = MyType::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
    do_stuff(value);
}
```
See also the documentation for [ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#216-218)

#### fn [arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_take_rest)(u: [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Generate an arbitrary value of `Self` from the entirety of the given
unstructured data.

This is similar to Arbitrary::arbitrary, however it assumes that it is
the last consumer of the given data, and is thus able to consume it all
if it needs.  See also the documentation for
[ Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html).

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

This is useful for determining how many elements we should insert when creating an arbitrary collection.

The return value is similar to [ Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it returns a
tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number of bytes
required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation return `(0, None)` which is correct for any
type, but not ultimately that useful. Using `#[derive(Arbitrary)]` will
create a better implementation. If you are writing an `Arbitrary`
implementation by hand, and your type can be part of a dynamically sized
collection (such as `Vec`), you are strongly encouraged to override this
default with a better implementation, and also override
[ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint).

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-implement-this)How to implement this

If the size hint calculation is a trivial constant and does not recurse
into any other `size_hint` call, you should implement it in `size_hint`:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct(u8);
impl<'a> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        let buf = &mut [0];
        u.fill_buffer(buf)?;
        Ok(SomeStruct(buf[0]))
    }
    #[inline]
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        let _ = depth;
        (1, Some(1))
    }
}
```
Otherwise, it should instead be implemented in [ try_size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.try_size_hint),
and the

`size_hint` implementation should forward to it:```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Result, Unstructured};
struct SomeStruct<A, B> {
    a: A,
    b: B,
}
impl<'a, A: Arbitrary<'a>, B: Arbitrary<'a>> Arbitrary<'a> for SomeStruct<A, B> {
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of try_size_hint
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default, always valid `(0, None)`
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::and(
                <A as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <B as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#invariant)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/lib.rs.html#423-425)

#### fn [try_size_hint](https://docs.rs#method.try_size_hint)(
    depth: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>), [MaxRecursionReached](https://docs.rs/struct.MaxRecursionReached.html)>

Get a size hint for how many bytes out of an `Unstructured` this type
needs to construct itself.

Unlike [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), this function keeps the information that the
recursion limit was reached. This is required to “short circuit” the
calculation and avoid exponential blowup with recursive structures.

If you are implementing [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) for a struct that could be
recursive, you should implement

`try_size_hint` and call the
`try_size_hint` when recursingThe return value is similar to [ core::iter::Iterator::size_hint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.size_hint): it
returns a tuple where the first element is a lower bound on the number
of bytes required, and the second element is an optional upper bound.

The default implementation returns the value of [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html) which is
correct for any type, but might lead to exponential blowup when dealing
with recursive types.

[§](https://docs.rs#invariant-1)Invariant

It must be possible to construct every possible output using only inputs
of lengths bounded by these parameters. This applies to both
[ Arbitrary::arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#tymethod.arbitrary) and

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest)

`Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest`This is trivially true for `(0, None)`. To restrict this further, it
must be proven that all inputs that are now excluded produced redundant
outputs which are still possible to produce using the reduced input
space.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-implement-try_size_hint)When to implement `try_size_hint`

If you 100% know that the type you are implementing `Arbitrary` for is
not a recursive type, or your implementation is not transitively calling
any other `size_hint` methods, you may implement [ size_hint](https://docs.rs/size_hint/index.html), and the
default

`try_size_hint` implementation will use it.Note that if you are implementing `Arbitrary` for a generic type, you
cannot guarantee the lack of type recursion!

Otherwise, when there is possible type recursion, you should implement
`try_size_hint` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-depth-parameter)The `depth` parameter

When implementing `try_size_hint`, you need to use
[ arbitrary::size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth)](https://docs.rs/size_hint/fn.try_recursion_guard.html)
to prevent potential infinite recursion when calculating size hints for
potentially recursive types:

```
use arbitrary::{size_hint, Arbitrary, MaxRecursionReached, Unstructured};
// This can potentially be a recursive type if `L` or `R` contain
// something like `Box<Option<MyEither<L, R>>>`!
enum MyEither<L, R> {
    Left(L),
    Right(R),
}
impl<'a, L, R> Arbitrary<'a> for MyEither<L, R>
where
    L: Arbitrary<'a>,
    R: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured) -> arbitrary::Result<Self> {
        // ...
    }
    fn size_hint(depth: usize) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
        // Return the value of `try_size_hint`
        //
        // If the recursion fails, return the default `(0, None)` range,
        // which is always valid.
        Self::try_size_hint(depth).unwrap_or_default()
    }
    fn try_size_hint(depth: usize) -> Result<(usize, Option<usize>), MaxRecursionReached> {
        // Protect against potential infinite recursion with
        // `try_recursion_guard`.
        size_hint::try_recursion_guard(depth, |depth| {
            // If we aren't too deep, then `recursion_guard` calls
            // this closure, which implements the natural size hint.
            // Don't forget to use the new `depth` in all nested
            // `try_size_hint` calls! We recommend shadowing the
            // parameter, like what is done here, so that you can't
            // accidentally use the wrong depth.
            Ok(size_hint::or(
                <L as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
                <R as Arbitrary>::try_size_hint(depth)?,
            ))
        })
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Unstructured in arbitrary - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/arbitrary/latest/target-redirect/arbitrary/struct.Unstructured.html

`pub struct Unstructured<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A source of unstructured data.

An `Unstructured` helps `Arbitrary` implementations interpret raw data
(typically provided by a fuzzer) as a “DNA string” that describes how to
construct the `Arbitrary` type. The goal is that a small change to the “DNA
string” (the raw data wrapped by an `Unstructured`) results in a small
change to the generated `Arbitrary` instance. This helps a fuzzer
efficiently explore the `Arbitrary`’s input space.

`Unstructured` is deterministic: given the same raw data, the same series of
API calls will return the same results (modulo system resource constraints,
like running out of memory). However, `Unstructured` does not guarantee
anything beyond that: it makes not guarantee that it will yield bytes from
the underlying data in any particular order.

You shouldn’t generally need to use an `Unstructured` unless you are writing
a custom `Arbitrary` implementation by hand, instead of deriving it. Mostly,
you should just be passing it through to nested `Arbitrary::arbitrary`
calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Imagine you were writing a color conversion crate. You might want to write fuzz tests that take a random RGB color and assert various properties, run functions and make sure nothing panics, etc.

Below is what translating the fuzzer’s raw input into an `Unstructured` and
using that to generate an arbitrary RGB color might look like:

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
/// An RGB color.
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
pub struct Rgb {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
}
// Get the raw bytes from the fuzzer.
let raw_data: &[u8] = get_input_from_fuzzer();
// Wrap it in an `Unstructured`.
let mut unstructured = Unstructured::new(raw_data);
// Generate an `Rgb` color and run our checks.
if let Ok(rgb) = Rgb::arbitrary(&mut unstructured) {
    run_my_color_conversion_checks(rgb);
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#76-766)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Unstructured%3C'a%3E)### impl<'a> [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#76-766)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Unstructured%3C'a%3E)

### impl<'a> [Unstructured](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html)<'a>

Get the number of remaining bytes of underlying data that are still available.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3]);
// Initially have three bytes of data.
assert_eq!(u.len(), 3);
// Generating a `bool` consumes one byte from the underlying data, so
// we are left with two bytes afterwards.
let _ = bool::arbitrary(&mut u);
assert_eq!(u.len(), 2);
```
Is the underlying unstructured data exhausted?

`unstructured.is_empty()` is the same as `unstructured.len() == 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
// Initially, we are not empty.
assert!(!u.is_empty());
// Generating a `u32` consumes all four bytes of the underlying data, so
// we become empty afterwards.
let _ = u32::arbitrary(&mut u);
assert!(u.is_empty());
```
Generate an arbitrary instance of `A`.

This is simply a helper method that is equivalent to `<A as Arbitrary>::arbitrary(self)`. This helper is a little bit more concise,
and can be used in situations where Rust’s type inference will figure
out what `A` should be.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
struct MyType {
    // ...
}
fn do_stuff(value: MyType) {
    // ...
}
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
// Rust's type inference can figure out that `value` should be of type
// `MyType` here:
let value = u.arbitrary()?;
do_stuff(value);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#214-223)#### pub fn [arbitrary_len](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_len)<ElementType>(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#214-223)

#### pub fn [arbitrary_len](https://docs.rs#method.arbitrary_len)<ElementType>(&mut self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

Get the number of elements to insert when building up a collection of
arbitrary `ElementType`s.

This uses the [ <ElementType as Arbitrary>::size_hint](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.size_hint) method to smartly
choose a length such that we most likely have enough underlying bytes to
construct that many arbitrary

`ElementType`s.This should only be called within an `Arbitrary` implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Result, Unstructured};
impl<'a, T> Arbitrary<'a> for MyCollection<T>
where
    T: Arbitrary<'a>,
{
    fn arbitrary(u: &mut Unstructured<'a>) -> Result<Self> {
        // Get the number of `T`s we should insert into our collection.
        let len = u.arbitrary_len::<T>()?;
        // And then create a collection of that length!
        let mut my_collection = MyCollection::with_capacity(len);
        for _ in 0..len {
            let element = T::arbitrary(u)?;
            my_collection.insert(element);
        }
        Ok(my_collection)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#300-307)#### pub fn [int_in_range](https://docs.rs#method.int_in_range)<T>(&mut self, range: [RangeInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.RangeInclusive.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#300-307)

#### pub fn [int_in_range](https://docs.rs#method.int_in_range)<T>(&mut self, range: [RangeInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.RangeInclusive.html)<T>) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>

Generate an integer within the given range.

Do not use this to generate the size of a collection. Use
`arbitrary_len` instead.

The probability distribution of the return value is not necessarily uniform.

Returns `range.start()`, not an error,
if this `Unstructured` [is empty](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html#method.is_empty).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `range.start > range.end`. That is, the given range must be
non-empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use arbitrary::{Arbitrary, Unstructured};
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
let x: i32 = u.int_in_range(-5_000..=-1_000)?;
assert!(-5_000 <= x);
assert!(x <= -1_000);
```
Choose one of the given choices.

This should only be used inside of `Arbitrary` implementations.

The probability distribution of choices is not necessarily uniform.

Returns the first choice, not an error,
if this `Unstructured` [is empty](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html#method.is_empty).

Returns an error if no choices are provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Selecting from an array of choices:

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0]);
let choices = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g'];
let choice = u.choose(&choices).unwrap();
println!("chose {}", choice);
```
An error is returned if no choices are provided:

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0]);
let choices: [char; 0] = [];
let result = u.choose(&choices);
assert!(result.is_err());
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#504-510)#### pub fn [choose_index](https://docs.rs#method.choose_index)(&mut self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

#### pub fn [choose_index](https://docs.rs#method.choose_index)(&mut self, len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

Choose a value in `0..len`.

The probability distribution of return values is not necessarily uniform.

Returns zero, not an error, if this `Unstructured` [is empty](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html#method.is_empty).

Returns an error if the `len` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

Using Fisher–Yates shuffle shuffle to generate an arbitrary permutation.

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0]);
let mut permutation = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g'];
let mut to_permute = &mut permutation[..];
while to_permute.len() > 1 {
    let idx = u.choose_index(to_permute.len()).unwrap();
    to_permute.swap(0, idx);
    to_permute = &mut to_permute[1..];
}
println!("permutation: {:?}", permutation);
```
An error is returned if the length is zero:

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0]);
let array: [i32; 0] = [];
let result = u.choose_index(array.len());
assert!(result.is_err());
```
Generate a boolean which is true with probability approximately the given ratio.

Returns true, not an error, if this `Unstructured` [is empty](https://docs.rs/struct.Unstructured.html#method.is_empty).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics when the numerator and denominator do not meet these constraints:

- `0 < numerator <= denominator`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

Generate a boolean that is `true` five sevenths of the time:

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&my_data);
if u.ratio(5, 7)? {
    // Take this branch approximately 5/7 of the time.
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#577-585)#### pub fn [fill_buffer](https://docs.rs#method.fill_buffer)(&mut self, buffer: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#577-585)

#### pub fn [fill_buffer](https://docs.rs#method.fill_buffer)(&mut self, buffer: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Fill a `buffer` with bytes from the underlying raw data.

This should only be called within an `Arbitrary` implementation. This is
a very low-level operation. You should generally prefer calling nested
`Arbitrary` implementations like `<Vec<u8>>::arbitrary` and
`String::arbitrary` over using this method directly.

If this `Unstructured` does not have enough underlying data to fill the
whole `buffer`, it pads the buffer out with zeros.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
let mut buf = [0; 2];
assert!(u.fill_buffer(&mut buf).is_ok());
assert_eq!(buf, [1, 2]);
assert!(u.fill_buffer(&mut buf).is_ok());
assert_eq!(buf, [3, 4]);
assert!(u.fill_buffer(&mut buf).is_ok());
assert_eq!(buf, [0, 0]);
```
Provide `size` bytes from the underlying raw data.

This should only be called within an `Arbitrary` implementation. This is
a very low-level operation. You should generally prefer calling nested
`Arbitrary` implementations like `<Vec<u8>>::arbitrary` and
`String::arbitrary` over using this method directly.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-9)Example

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3, 4]);
assert!(u.bytes(2).unwrap() == &[1, 2]);
assert!(u.bytes(2).unwrap() == &[3, 4]);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#635-637)

Peek at `size` number of bytes of the underlying raw input.

Does not consume the bytes, only peeks at them.

Returns `None` if there are not `size` bytes left in the underlying raw
input.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3]);
assert_eq!(u.peek_bytes(0).unwrap(), []);
assert_eq!(u.peek_bytes(1).unwrap(), [1]);
assert_eq!(u.peek_bytes(2).unwrap(), [1, 2]);
assert_eq!(u.peek_bytes(3).unwrap(), [1, 2, 3]);
assert!(u.peek_bytes(4).is_none());
```
Consume all of the rest of the remaining underlying bytes.

Returns a slice of all the remaining, unconsumed bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
use arbitrary::Unstructured;
let mut u = Unstructured::new(&[1, 2, 3]);
let mut remaining = u.take_rest();
assert_eq!(remaining, [1, 2, 3]);
```

Provide an iterator over elements for constructing a collection from all the remaining bytes.

This is useful for implementing [ Arbitrary::arbitrary_take_rest](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html#method.arbitrary_take_rest) on collections
since the implementation is simply

`u.arbitrary_take_rest_iter()?.collect()`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#748-765)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/arbitrary/unstructured.rs.html#748-765)

Call the given function an arbitrary number of times.

The function is given this `Unstructured` so that it can continue to
generate arbitrary data and structures.

You may optionaly specify minimum and maximum bounds on the number of times the function is called.

You may break out of the loop early by returning
`Ok(std::ops::ControlFlow::Break)`. To continue the loop, return
`Ok(std::ops::ControlFlow::Continue)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

Panics if `min > max`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-12)Example

Call a closure that generates an arbitrary type inside a context an arbitrary number of times:

```
use arbitrary::{Result, Unstructured};
use std::ops::ControlFlow;
enum Type {
    /// A boolean type.
    Bool,
    /// An integer type.
    Int,
    /// A list of the `i`th type in this type's context.
    List(usize),
}
fn arbitrary_types_context(u: &mut Unstructured) -> Result<Vec<Type>> {
    let mut context = vec![];
    u.arbitrary_loop(Some(10), Some(20), |u| {
        let num_choices = if context.is_empty() {
            2
        } else {
            3
        };
        let ty = match u.int_in_range::<u8>(1..=num_choices)? {
            1 => Type::Bool,
            2 => Type::Int,
            3 => Type::List(u.int_in_range(0..=context.len() - 1)?),
            _ => unreachable!(),
        };
        context.push(ty);
        Ok(ControlFlow::Continue(()))
    })?;
    // The number of loop iterations are constrained by the min/max
    // bounds that we provided.
    assert!(context.len() >= 10);
    assert!(context.len() <= 20);
    Ok(context)
}
```
